prompt: How does the lesson define vendor lock-in?
hint: Something you could estimate in hours.

choices.text: Using a proprietary service anywhere in the system
choices.why: That makes lock-in a yes-or-no property. The lesson turns it into a quantity.

choices.text: The cost of switching away
choices.why: Right: hours of rewriting, data to move, a contract to wait out, people to retrain. The more it costs, the deeper the lock-in.

choices.text: A contract longer than a year
choices.why: A contract term is one kind of lock-in among four, not the definition.

choices.text: Depending on a vendor that competitors also use
choices.why: Sharing a vendor with competitors says nothing about what leaving it would cost.

prompt: Why does the lesson say "we should avoid vendor lock-in" decides nothing?
hint: Can it be followed, and when would you stop?

choices.text: It gives no price for avoiding lock-in
choices.why: Right: without a price, a team cannot tell when portability stops being worth what it costs.

choices.text: Lock-in is rare in modern cloud systems
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: every choice locks you into something.

choices.text: Architects disagree about what lock-in means
choices.why: The trouble is the opposite: nobody disagrees with the sentence, which is the sign it is a slogan.

choices.text: It applies to vendors and Coreto mostly builds its own
choices.why: Coreto depends on a cloud database and a payment gateway; the problem is with the slogan, not the company.

prompt: Match each kind of lock-in to its instance at Coreto.
hint: Data is what you would move; interface is what you would rewrite.

pairs.right: The stored cards that let returning buyers pay in one tap
Catalogue code calling the database's own query interface in many places
The few engineers who know the database's query model

right_distractors: The size of the monthly cloud bill

prompt: The Catalogue team estimates 1,400 hours to leave the managed document database. At R$ 150 an hour, what is the switching cost, in reais?
Of the four kinds of lock-in, which does the lesson say a team controls most, and why?
hint: Where is it decided, and how often?

choices.text: Contract, since it is negotiated by Coreto
choices.why: A contract is decided once, at signing; after that the team has little say.

choices.text: Data, since the team chooses the storage format
choices.why: Data is mostly decided when the vendor is chosen, along with its export terms.

choices.text: Skills, since the team can train anyone it hires
choices.why: The lesson says skills accumulate on their own, which is the opposite of control.

choices.text: Interface: decided in the code, call by call
choices.why: Right: each time somebody writes a direct call to the vendor's API, the switching cost grows a little.

prompt: Leaving the payment gateway would cost R$ 135,000, and Coreto puts the chance of a switch at 35% in three years. What is the expected cost, in reais?
The document database has the larger switching cost, R$ 210,000 against R$ 135,000. Which lock-in should Davi spend more attention on, and why?
hint: Weigh each by how likely the switch is.

choices.text: The database, because it would cost more to leave
choices.why: That reads the switching cost alone; at 10% its expected cost is R$ 21,000.

choices.text: The gateway: its expected cost is more than twice the database's
choices.why: Right: R$ 47,250 against R$ 21,000. The lock-in most likely to be tested is the gateway.

choices.text: Neither, since both are below one engineer-year
choices.why: Size against an engineer-year is a caution about catastrophe, not a reason to ignore either.

choices.text: Both equally, since lock-in is lock-in
choices.why: That is the slogan again; the expected costs differ by more than a factor of two.

prompt: In your lock-in sheet, D2 (=B2*C2) shows 2100000 for the document database. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Lesson 1's trouble section made this exact mistake on purpose.

choices.text: B2 was pasted as text
choices.why: Text in B2 would give #VALUE!, not a number a hundred times too large.

choices.text: C2 holds 10 instead of 10%
choices.why: Right: R$ 210,000 × 10 is a hundred times R$ 210,000 × 10%, with no error on the screen. Check one row by hand.

choices.text: The spreadsheet is set to another language
choices.why: A language mismatch breaks function names or decimal commas with an error; this product has neither.

choices.text: The switching cost was typed in cents
choices.why: Cents would make it a hundred times too large in B2 itself, which would show 21000000.

prompt: The CFO reads the sheet and asks: "So leaving the database will cost us R$ 21,000?" What is the accurate answer?
hint: What happens in each of the two possible futures?

choices.text: Yes, over three years
choices.why: Nothing is spread: either Coreto stays and pays nothing, or it leaves and pays about R$ 210,000.

choices.text: Yes, provided the probability estimate is right
choices.why: Even with a perfect probability, no future has a bill of R$ 21,000.

choices.text: No: it is R$ 210,000, because the sheet is wrong
choices.why: The sheet is right; R$ 210,000 is the cost if the switch happens, and the 10% weighs it.

choices.text: No: it is a weight, not a bill
choices.why: Right: the expected cost compares options on one scale. On any single lock-in, the outcome is all or nothing.

prompt: Expected cost = probability × the ___ cost, what leaving would cost if you left.
hint: What leaving would cost, if you left.

prompt: An adapter for the document database takes 300 hours to build and 40 hours a year to keep up. At R$ 150 an hour, what does it cost over three years, in reais?
Row 3 of the sheet has an expected cost of 47250 in D3 and portability of 24000 in E3. What does =IF(E3<D3,"pay for portability","accept the lock-in") return?

choices.text: accept the lock-in
choices.why: That is row 2's answer, where portability (63000) exceeds the expected cost (21000).

choices.text: #VALUE!, because the text has spaces
choices.why: Text in quotes may hold spaces; the formula returns one of its two strings.

choices.text: pay for portability
choices.why: Right: R$ 24,000 removes an expected R$ 47,250, about half, so the gateway's lock-in is bought out.

choices.text: 23250, the difference between the two cells
choices.why: IF returns one of the two values it was given; it does not subtract.

prompt: The adapter costs R$ 63,000 and switching away from the database would cost R$ 210,000. Above what probability of switching, in percent, would the adapter pay for itself?
Besides its hours, what cost of the database adapter does the lesson say no sheet holds?
hint: What can an adapter written for any database expose?

choices.text: It slows every query noticeably
choices.why: The lesson does not claim a performance cost; its point is about features.

choices.text: It exposes the lowest common denominator
choices.why: Right: portability to any database is bought with the features that made this one attractive.

choices.text: The provider charges extra for indirect access
choices.why: Nothing in the example has the provider charging for how Coreto structures its code.

choices.text: It makes the data impossible to export
choices.why: An adapter changes how code reaches the database; it does not touch export.

prompt: Davi writes down the decision to accept the database lock-in, with what would reopen it. Why bother, if nothing is being built?
hint: How does an unwritten decision look a year later?

choices.text: To satisfy an audit requirement
choices.why: No audit is involved; the note is for the team that meets this lock-in later.

choices.text: So the vendor sees Coreto is ready to leave
choices.why: The note is internal, and it says Coreto is staying unless something changes.

choices.text: Unwritten, an accepted lock-in looks like an accident
choices.why: Right: and the triggers — a price rise, the product retired, a chance above 30% — say when to look again.

choices.text: To have a reason ready if the switch happens and goes badly
choices.why: The note is a decision with its conditions, written for the people who revisit it, not a defence.

prompt: Put the steps of pricing a lock-in in the order the lesson takes them.
hint: You cannot weigh a cost you never estimated.
items: Estimate the switching cost in hours
Judge the probability of switching, with reasons
Multiply them into an expected cost
Price the portability that would avoid it
Compare, and write down the decision and its trigger
trap: Starting from portability is the slogan's order: paying to avoid a lock-in before anybody has said what the lock-in would cost.

prompt: Six months later the database's provider announces a price rise, and the Catalogue lead now puts the chance of leaving above 30%. By Davi's note, what follows?

choices.text: Reopen it: above 30%, the R$ 63,000 adapter now pays for itself
choices.why: Right: the expected cost now exceeds the portability, so the comparison flips.

choices.text: Nothing, since the lock-in was accepted in writing
choices.why: The note named exactly this as a trigger; writing it down was what made revisiting possible.

choices.text: Switch databases straight away
choices.why: A higher chance of switching is not a switch; the question is whether the adapter now pays.

choices.text: Raise the switching cost estimate to match
choices.why: A price rise changes the probability, not the hours it would take to leave.

prompt: Which kinds of lock-in are decided once, at signing, by the lesson's account? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are settled with the vendor; two keep moving.

choices.text: Data
choices.why: Yes: the format and the export terms come with the vendor you choose.

choices.text: Interface
choices.why: Interface lock-in is decided in the code, each time somebody writes a call.

choices.text: Contract
choices.why: Yes: notice, term and fees are fixed when it is signed.

choices.text: Skills
choices.why: Skills accumulate on their own over the years, with no single moment of decision.

prompt: The sheet treats portability as if it removed the switching cost entirely. Which way does that simplification lean?
hint: With the interface in place, does leaving cost nothing?

choices.text: Towards portability, since a switch still costs something
choices.why: Right: so near a break-even, estimate the remaining switching cost and compare that instead.

choices.text: Against portability, since its yearly upkeep is ignored
choices.why: The upkeep is in the sheet: 40 hours a year for the adapter, three times.

choices.text: Neither way, since it cancels out
choices.why: It removes a cost from the portability side only, so it does not cancel.

choices.text: Towards accepting lock-in, since probabilities are rounded
choices.why: Rounding the probabilities is a separate matter; this simplification concerns what portability achieves.
